newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine deputies debate on easing unemployment.
newsitem.headline: Argentine deputies debate on easing unemployment.

text.p: The lower house of the Argentine Congress began an opposition-sponsored debate on Wednesday about the country's 17.1 percent unemployment -- which has fueled two general strikes in two months.
The ruling Peronist Party majority had threatened to stay away from the debate and deprive it of a quorum, but Peronist whip Jorge Matzkin changed his mind.
"Our position is that we will listen to any idea, wherever it comes from, that might help create just one job," he told reporters before the debate began on Wednesday.
Matzkin warned that no concrete proposals had been tabled and said: "Expectations are high for this debate, I just hope they are not disappointed."

But the Radical Party, the biggest opposition force, hopes it will produce legislation to help create jobs, which Radical former Economy Minister Jesus Rodriguez told the House were being lost at the rate of 30 an hour.

The Radical leader in the house, Federico Storani, told a news conference earlier: "We don't want this debate to be a political tournament, we want a commitment from the government to have an Employment Emergency Law in two weeks' time."
The job debate has moved to Congress after weeks of public protest: a 24-hour general strike in August, a "blackout" on September 12 and a 36-hour general strike last week.

Protest initially grew because of Peronist government tax austerity measures -- new taxes and worker benefit cuts. But, with those laws passed by Congress, protest has shifted to a government drive for more flexible labor laws and for the deregulation of union-controlled mandatory health plans.
Storani said President Carlos Menem's drive for new labor laws will "only destabilize employment and create social and political conflict."

Trade unionists, once a close ally of the Peronists, are now on a war footing over what they see as an attempt by Menem to deprive them of a role in collective wage bargaining and of $2.5 billion a year of health-plan income.
Union leaders including Rodolfo Daer, secretary general of the main labor federation, the CGT, were blocked entry to the Chamber of Deputies for the unemployment debate.
"If that's the order, it's because they have something to hide, they don't want to debate this problem in front of the people," said hardline union boss Hugo Moyano.
